WORKED EXAMPLES
Courage +
By using a close-up on Sayyid while the crowd cheers, Grentell positions us to feel his personal triumph, revealing the film's view that courage is both gradually built over time and expressed in the moment. The close-up isolates Sayyid from the celebrating crowd. We see his face rather than the group, which conveys an atmosphere of private achievement within a public moment. This choice reveals the view that belonging is something you earn quietly, not something handed to you.
Language +
By using a medium shot of Sayyid and Neil on either side of the cake display, Grentell lets us observe a moment of connection across cultural difference, revealing the film's view that language is not only words but the willingness to meet someone where they are. The framing keeps both figures equal in the shot. Neither dominates the other. This choice highlights how the film values exchange over assimilation, and suggests that belonging begins with small acts of recognition.
+ More examples coming
Belonging +
By using a slow pan across Saroo's childhood neighbourhood as he returns, Davis positions us to feel the weight of memory and loss, revealing the film's view that belonging is something you carry inside you rather than something a place can give back. The camera moves slowly, as though reluctant to arrive. We observe the gap between the place Saroo imagined and the place that exists. This choice conveys an atmosphere of tender dislocation, highlighting how the search for home is also a search for self.

The Merger -- a sports film as a vehicle for social change +
Inside the story: The Merger -- a sports film as a vehicle for social change Published: May 7, 2019 | The Conversation Set against the political backdrop of Australia's refugee policy and the racism it generates, Mark Grentell's The Merger (2018) uses the genre of the sports film to explore -- and ultimately challenge -- the attitudes around this hotly contested topic. Adapted from a comedy play of the same name, written by and starring Damian Callinan, The Merger draws on the tropes we expect of the sports film -- world, character, structure, theme -- to tell a poignant, and important, tale of how a struggling Aussie Rules footy team (The Roosters) in an equally struggling town (Bodgy Creek) learns to accept people for who they are and what they can offer a community. Structurally, a hallmark of the sports film is its dramatic shape as a rite of passage. A protagonist faces a problem and grows out of it, becoming a new person who is able to prove their value to the world. The dramatic goal of winning a game or tournament represents triumph for the protagonist, and the team or town. In The Merger, Troy (Callinan) -- a disgraced local blamed for the town's decline -- is drafted in by naive teenager Neil (Rafferty Grierson) to help The Roosters improve their game -- literally and, as we come to learn, morally. Troy is also given a chance for redemption -- a second go at saving the town he allegedly destroyed. Not surprisingly, Troy's character arc sees him invited back into the community. A mirror to the core thematic story of accepting refugees, this storyline sees Bodgy Creek's residents understand and forgive his past and value him for who he is now. The structural and thematic connection between Troy and Neil is important to note here. The son of "leftie" Angie (Kate Mulvany) -- whose father-in-law, Bull (John Howard), happens to be The Roosters' president (and a racist) -- Neil is young, naive and innocent. To him, Troy is just a man who has the skills The Roosters need -- so why are people being so nasty to him? A DRAMATIC QUEST Neil provides the initial "call to adventure" for Troy, willing him into the story. Neil's mother runs a local refugee centre, and it is through this that The Merger's story really begins. A grant scheme to employ refugees is suggested as a way of finally getting the clubhouse fixed up. Here, the film's title is used to punctuate the dramatic question of the story: do you want to merge, or do you want to fold? In terms of story world, the setting of Bodgy Creek is important. A former award winning "tidy town", it is now brimming with rubbish and morale is at an all-time low. Here, world is used purposely to reflect the film's central theme -- a place where people have given up on not only themselves, but also on each other. NARRATIVE NEED FOR CHANGE In screenwriting terms, something has to change -- people, places, attitudes, values. In the sports film, the team and its desire for success (plot) reflects a deeper need for meaning and renewed hope (theme). This is especially important for The Merger's political context of refugees being settled in Australia, where footy acts as a vehicle for bringing the characters together and teaching them -- and the audience -- about respect and reciprocity. The sports film requires a range of characters to explore these tensions. The openness and kindness of Troy, Angie and Neil is contrasted by club president Bull, a racist and traditionalist who only learns to "see properly" through the team's eventual success. Loutish antagonist Carpet Burn also represents the nasty, bigoted views of many Australians towards refugees. His character arc comes when he realises new player Sayyid (Fayssal Bazzi) is a better player than him, and that if he wants the team to succeed, they need to join forces. In all honesty, this conflict is a weak aspect of the film. There are not enough story beats to warrant the arcs of Bull and Carpet Burn. They change too easily, not pushed dramatically enough for an audience to feel this shift is justified. But the sentiment is there, and we know what the film is trying to say. Perhaps a hallmark of many Australian films, mateship triumphs as we see the team and its players unite for the benefit of footy. Attitudes and beliefs are swept aside in favour of what, for many, lies at the core of a "fair go" Australian life. Source: The Conversation, theconversation.com
